media.transcript: Thank you Madam Deputy Speaker. My constituent Maxwell has spinal muscular atrophy and needs a significant amount of personal care. Now, the Member for East Hampshire said that we assume it, but will the Minister confirm that the free personal care will be included for working-age disabled adults like Maxwell? Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker, and I'd like to thank the Honourable Member for raising his constituents' situation. situation. If he would like to send me details of that, I'll happily look into it and formally reply to him and his constituents. Baroness Casey's commission is working on recommendations for fixing the social care for everyone who needs it, including working age adults. I would just acknowledge that some of the challenges are different, so we need to take that into account as we move forward to the future system.

media.transcript: I'm kind of on borrowed time, is the truth of it. I'm so sorry. Thank you. I'm so sorry. No, sorry. You think you get used to it, you know? No, of course not. But yeah, I'm going to turn 32 on December the 3rd. I am unlikely to turn 33. That is 31 year old Sabrina Apeitz Grossman who is fighting a rare, aggressive, and life-threatening form of cancer. She's also now fighting the Ford government in court for refusing to fund a treatment that could save her life. It felt a little inhuman. People are just being told to die. That's the long and short of it. You know, you're just being told to die. Synovial sarcoma is a rare cancer that develops in soft tissue. It has spread to her lungs, making it stage four. She has tried multiple treatments in Canada, including chemotherapy and surgery, but she was told she has just 12 to 18 months to live. There is one treatment she hasn't tried and it could extend her life for years. It could even give her a chance of becoming cancer free. But it is only available in the US at a huge price tag of about $650,000. There is an Ontario program that she hoped could help. It is called the Out of Country Prior Approval Program, and it is intended to fund medical services outside of Canada. Sabrina appeared to meet all of the eligibility requirements, and she had high hopes she would get approval and get the treatment within weeks of applying. She was rejected. She is taking the province to court to overturn that decision. But every day of delay poses a real risk of narrowing the window in which she can receive the treatment according to her case. I mean, of course, it's a resource limited medical system. Like I'm not I do understand. There are a lot of expensive things we do for people, you know, people are in the ICU for weeks. And I have never for a moment thought to myself, gosh, I wish we hadn't spent that $500,000 to save somebody's life. Like, it's never crossed my mind. There aren't that many people who need these niche treatments, but when you are one of these people, you don't have another choice. Like, you know, it's not, I would rather not be doing this and not be asking for help, but at the same time, it's my life. Even more frustrating, on the same day she filed her court case, the province announced changes to its out-of-country funding rules, limiting which patients can qualify. So patients can now only qualify for treatments outside of Canada if the drug is temporarily unavailable here in Ontario. Otherwise, the drug and the administration of the drug must be publicly funded and approved here in Ontario. The province pointed to cost savings as one of the reasons for the change, saying this would limit the significant increase in requests for out-of-country treatments. They said it could save up to $170 million in additional annual costs and collectively save $5.2 billion annually. The change is retroactive to 2011 and basically it completely disqualifies Sabrina from the program. This is a heartbreaking commodification of patients and patient care. They are balancing their books on the backs of patients. The health minister's office told us it can't comment on Sabrina's case due to confidentiality reasons, but they also said Health Canada is responsible for determining whether a drug or therapy is authorized for use in Canada, including assessing its safety, efficacy and quality. You can find more on this story at thetrillium.ca.

media.transcript: We know affordability is top of mind, especially in Toronto. What makes these times even more challenging is living alone. Economists have dubbed it the single tax, and experts say it's becoming harder and harder to foot the bill. The actual people who are most likely to be in poverty are single people between the ages of 18 and 40. The average one-bedroom rent in Toronto right now is around $2,273 per month. Groceries cost about $360 per month for single-person households. Experts say solo shoppers also pay more because pack sizes are designed for larger households. Real estate agents say to budget for around $150 per month in utilities. That's almost $3,000 per month just to cover basic costs, which is almost the entire take-home of Toronto's last recorded median income. That's not even taking into account internet, transit, clothing or other expenses. The reality is now, many people living alone are struggling financially. The latest report from Foodbanks Canada shows single person households make up around 44% of food bank use. Single income households across the country and as well as provincially in most provinces, if not all, are the single largest household group accessing food banks. Richard Mattern with Foodbanks Canada says this is because of the rising costs of housing and food, not keeping up with wages. But he also notes a particular challenge one-person households face. single-person households in particular are one of the clearest examples of the gaps in our safety net. So when the job loss occurs or when working income is too low, they have other fewer supports to help, such as families with children have child tax benefits, seniors helps you use income benefits, single working age, single adults do not have those income benefits. And that gap in the system was also noted by the Wellesley Institute. A lot of the savings and a lot of the government strategies have been around families. So I think people haven't been thinking as hard and the needs of single people and they've dropped through the net. So when we're thinking about tax reform, we might want to think about the group who are most likely to be in poverty. When asked whether tax relief is currently being considered specifically for people living alone, the province pointed to broader affordability measures. In a statement, the Ministry of Finance said since 2018, we have not raised a single tax and have provided nearly $12 billion in support this year to help keep costs down for families and individuals. The province also noted it permanently cut the gas tax, raised minimum wage and reduced or eliminated income tax for 1.7 million low-income residents.

For weeks now, there have been student protests all across France and hundreds of high schools in response to poor school conditions like lack of tables, chairs, electricity, and massive staffing shortages. Protests grew into larger demonstrations as more people joined to protest high costs of living, including fuel prices, after bombs from the United States effectively forced the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The CGT, or the General Confederation of Labour, one of France's largest trade union centers, has called for lower prices, higher wages, and higher pensions. Meanwhile, this comes at a time when the Prime Minister, Sébastien Lacornu, has presented what has been called a belt-tightening budget for 2027 that attempts to attack France's deficit by freezing public sector wages and increasing taxes. So there's a lot of unrest. So then on Saturday, October 17th, over half a million people joined over 100 protests across France, which were largely peaceful, but there was some unrest, which has been characterized as violent rioting by most media outlets. There was also a lot of opportunistic rioting and looting, which people use the student protests and the general peaceful protests as a cover for their actions. At least 1,500 shops were vandalized, and as of the latest reporting, at least 2,400 French people were arrested. The Guardian is reporting that entire streets in Paris have been devastated and the pictures coming out of these protests are intense. This is the most unrest that France has faced in years. French police's forceful response has only exacerbated the anger of protesters. President Emmanuel Macron has blamed far-left activists and Trump has blamed immigrants because of course he has. So has anything come out of these protests? Yes, the French government had said they will deploy an additional 3,000 substitute teachers and will include students in further decision-making processes. They also scrapped plans to increase several university tuition fees that have been included in the new budget in response to the protests. But France is not the only country with protests. Let's talk about Spain. In Spain, activists have been protesting since September over housing prices and this was triggered after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her apartment after an investment fund increased her rent by 230%. Portuguese housing prices increased 124% from 2015 to 2024, which is nearly double the EU's average. Milan, Italy is also protesting the high cost of living. Total shot in the dark from one woman's opinion, but if people had their basic needs met, I don't think we'd be seeing protests at this level.

media.transcript: This is the best BMW nobody's talking about. And no, I'm not referring to the E90 platform as a whole. Plenty of people are talking about those already. The M3 parked itself in the Hall of Fame pretty much the moment it came out, thanks to its iconic V8 and its ability of doing absolutely anything you want it to. And then you get these. People also talk about these purely because they've aged like shit. These early SE cars are the ones you're most likely to see out and about today, largely because they outsold their competition when new. Dealers offered good deals on the smaller engine models and BMW's genius marketing convinced everyone that they deserve a BM instead of a trusty Mondeo or a not trusty Vectra. The thing is, those good deal E90s tended to have three numbers on the back and they said 3, 1 and 8. These four cylinder engines were available as a petrol or a diesel. Both are equally rubbish. The 2 litre diesels offered great economy but had the robustness of one of those red barrels on a Call of Duty map, instantly wiping away any of your precious fuel savings the moment they detonate. And they stink. The 2 litre petrols meanwhile had the internals made of the softest, saltiest feta cheese. Haunted by a blue mist of burnt oil wherever they go, these time bombs are mostly paired with Amish interiors and charmless wheels. It's all a bit of a massacre. However, not all E90s are born equal. Amongst the MTAC's icons and the Scrappy Challenge Specials is a car that I think might just be one of BMW's best ever. I'm of course talking about the iconic BMW 330i. But not just any 330, this specific 330. An early manual M Sport car with, and this is the most important bit, the often forgotten M52 engine. That's 255 big heavy ponies by the smoothest, creamiest, naturally aspirated Stray 6 BMW has ever produced. A bold claim, but I'll back it. The engine is mature and dynamically uninterrupted. It's ref happy all the way to 7000 RPM, but it's not intricate getting there. That was reserved for the M cars, which this isn't trying to beat. It does make a lovely noise though, and offers a bootload of torque to get you going. It's a quick car, this, definitely making up for its predecessors' downfalls. The rest of the driving dynamics are classic 3 series. It's reliable and predictable while also being efficient. You'll see north of 40mpg on the motorway while knowing it won't pop because the engine is famously reliable, unlike the M53 and the later 330s. And then you get the packaging. It's here where this car comes together. A beautifully contrasting interior, wood trim, M-Sport bumpers to sharpen up those looks, chrome kidney grills to give it class and those iconic period angel eye lights. This free 30 is what marketing was talking about when it convinced the everyman to buy a BM. It captured that BM magic in a much more mature way that its predecessors failed to do so. In turn it never really captured the attention of the real BM nerds, it's still focusing on the past, for better or for worse. Which is why today...

Trump just signed an executive order aimed at making housing more affordable. But what does that actually mean for Los Angeles homeowners and buyers?

Lower refinancing costs. Potential mortgage insurance savings. Fewer barriers to building new homes.

All promising ideas. But let’s be clear: This doesn’t mean interest rates are dropping tomorrow or that homes are suddenly becoming more affordable.

Implementation will take time, and the details matter.

As the owner of a Los Angeles real estate brokerage, I welcome efforts to make homeownership more accessible. But I also believe consumers deserve facts, not headlines.

Here’s my take on what the executive order could mean for our housing market.

onScreenText: AND WHILE THIS EXECUTIVE ORDER WON'T
media.transcript: Trump just signed an executive order to make housing more affordable, but will it actually make a difference in Los Angeles? I'm a little skeptical. I own a real estate brokerage called John Hart in LA, and I can tell you firsthand that affordability is one of the biggest challenges facing the housing market right now. We talk about this every single day here at John Hart. And while this executive order won't solve that problem overnight, there are a few things worth paying attention to. There's actually three things worth paying attention to. First, mortgage insurance. The order calls for a pilot program that could automatically eliminate mortgage insurance payments for eligible homeowners once they've built enough equity. That's money potentially going back into homeowners' pockets every single month. Second, refinancing. The administration wants to reduce refinancing expenses, including title insurance and appraisal costs. That could make refinancing less expensive for qualifying homeowners. Let's see if rates are going to go down anytime soon. Third, housing supply. The order encourages innovation in manufacturing housing, manufactured housing, and more standardized permitting. And anyone familiar with Los Angeles knows how challenging and expensive it is to build housing here. But here's what I want everyone to understand. This does not mean interest rates are going down anytime soon. It doesn't mean home prices are coming down as well. And it certainly doesn't mean these programs are available starting today. The details matter, and much of this still needs to be implemented. But I welcome conversations about making homeownership more affordable because the cost of housing has become one of the biggest obstacles to building wealth. And in a market like Los Angeles, look, let's face it, where affordability has kept so many people on the sidelines, even incremental savings can make a big difference. My advice, don't make real estate decisions based on headlines. Please understand the numbers, understand the opportunities and surround yourself with John Harder. people that understand exactly how to do both. Because regardless of what happens in Washington, opportunities still exist right here in Los Angeles. You just need to know where to look.
